newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Israeli missile defence comes with big price tag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Israeli missile defence comes with big price tag.

text.p: A successful test of the Arrow missile last month put Israel one step closer to developing a defence against enemy missiles, but its projected cost of only $1.6 billion could be just a flight of fancy.
Project officials say an operational version of the missile, funded jointly by Israel and the United States, will be ready in 1998, 10 years after the programme was launched.
The budget estimate published by Israeli Defence Ministry would cover expenses through 2005 when Israel expects to field enough batteries to intercept missiles fired at any part of its territory.

"Getting to that stage of the project on $1.6 billion is a ridiculous estimate. The Arrow will cost many times that figure," said Reuven Pedatzur, a political scientist who has researched the feasibility of the Arrow missile.
The Arrow began as an adjunct of the U.S. Strategic Defence Initiative, or "Star Wars", but took on a life of its own when Iraq fired dozens of Scud missiles at Israel in the 1991 Gulf War.

The Iraqi missiles caused few casualties but the psychological effect on Israel's civilian population and the ineffectiveness of U.S. Patriot missiles in intercepting the Scuds made the missile defence project a top priority.

The Arrow's radar system, developed by a subsidiary of Israel Aircraft Industry, is designed to track missiles fired at Israel and guide the Arrow, travelling at nearly three km (two miles) per second, to within four metres (13 ft) of an incoming missile.
Somewhere between 10 km (six miles) and 40 km (25 miles) above the ground, the Arrow is supposed to intercept the incoming missile.

Pedatzur, a reserve air force pilot who spent three years studying the Arrow project, said development and production of the radar, missiles and a "command and control system" that will coordinate the operations of multiple missile batteries would top $6 billion.
"I don't know where he gets these figures. They are completely unfounded," said David Ivri, director-general of the Defence Ministry and a prime mover in the missile defence project.

Ivri told Reuters Israel was spending roughly $100 million a year on developing the Arrow, with $40 million of that money coming from the United States. Security sources estimate the two countries have poured $500 million into the project since 1991.
Israel receives $1.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid. An agreement between the two countries gives the United States access to the Arrow's research and development data.
Ivri said the $100 million a year would allow Israel to meet its 1998 target date for the current programme and subsequent projects.
Israel, he said, would initially deploy two missile batteries to protect the populous central and northern regions of the country. Ivri would not say how many missiles each battery would contain.
The Defence Ministry published the $1.6 billion estimate for the first time last month after years of media speculation, but it did not provide an itemised budget.
Pedatzur said project officials deliberately under-calculated the cost.
"Had they given the real numbers, the people who make the decisions would have realised this project is impossible to finance. They want to ensure that the project continues," he told Reuters.

Pedatzur compares the Arrow with Israel's ill-fated Lavi fighter plane. Israel spent $1.5 billion on the Lavi programme before cancelling it in 1987 over speculation that development alone would reach $2.6 billion.

The number of Arrow missiles Israel will finally deploy is a key issue in the argument over budget estimates. According to Jane's defence magazine Israel would need more than 1,200 Arrows to defend against a combined Arab arsenal of 2,000 to 3,000 medium-range missiles.
The price of each Arrow is expected to top $2 million so that amassing a full arsenal alone would put Israel over the $1.6 billion budget estimate for the whole Arrow programme.

Pedatzur said the large difference between the cost of the Arrow missile and a Scud missile, estimated at $500,000, would encourage Arab states to stockpile more and more missiles while Israel would be unable to match the pace.
Project backers say in response that Israeli aircraft would destroy much of the Arab arsenal in a future conflict before the missiles are ever launched.
Defence officials say Pedatzur is obsessed with disproving the Arrow's feasibility but he is not alone in questioning the feasibility of the programme.
"People on the inside, mainly from the air force, have raised some of the same questions he (Pedatzur) raises about the programme," said a retired senior officer who refused to be named.
"But as long as it appears that Arrow has a chance to succeed, no one on the inside is going to go public with the criticism," he said.
